beads.title: Guard index eviction on peer removal so a departing peer cannot evict its successor
beads.description: At commit a8b023c063b608fcead5446f3d885c4fc847c944 upstream makes every node-index eviction in ipn/ipnlocal/node_backend.go conditional through a deleteIfOwned helper: an entry in nodeByAddr, nodeByKey, nodeByWGString, nodeByStableID or nodeByName is deleted only if it still maps to the node being removed or replaced. The reason is concrete. Control can reassign a churning ephemeral peer's Tailscale IP (or its MagicDNS name) to a newer peer and deliver the new peer's upsert BEFORE the old peer's removal -- either in an earlier MapResponse, or reordered inside one batch by the NodeID sort in netmap.MutationsFromMapResponse. An unconditional delete then wipes the new owner's entry. The peer map itself stayed correct in every ordering, so WireGuard kept the peer and handshakes succeeded, but WhoIs by IP failed until the next full netmap; on app connectors that surfaced as 'peerapi: unknown peer' with a restart as the only recovery. This repository already does the guarded thing on the upsert path and says so. PeerDb::upsert in ts_runtime/src/peer_tracker/peer_db.rs retracts from disco_idx, name_idx, ip_idx and route_idx only after checking the entry is still its own -- 'never clobber another peer's', a comment added after an unguarded version used to assert! and panic the actor under concurrent joins. IndexState::remove, the REMOVAL path in the same file, does not. It calls nk_idx.remove, stableid_idx.remove, control_idx.remove, ip_idx.remove for both tailnet addresses, and disco_idx.remove unconditionally; only the hostname half of name_idx and the inactive disco key are guarded, and the comment on the guarded one ('for the same reason as every other index above') describes indexes that are not in fact guarded. The fqdn half of name_idx is unguarded too. The exposure is not theoretical, and it is worse here than the ordering upstream defends against: PeerTracker::apply_peer_update in ts_runtime/src/peer_tracker/mod.rs applies a Delta's upserts first and its removals second, unconditionally, so the intra-batch ordering that broke Go is the ordering this tree always uses. A peer that inherits a departing peer's tailnet IP is installed in ip_idx and then evicted by the departing peer's removal, after which PeerTracker::peer_by_tailnet_ip, the whois built on it, and every peerAPI source check that resolves through that index fail for a peer that is present and handshaking. disco_idx has the same shape, and there the cost is the new peer's direct path. The work is one helper plus its call sites: make each retraction in IndexState::remove conditional on the entry still mapping to the id being removed, including the fqdn half of name_idx. Test the orderings that actually differ -- upsert-then-remove within one Delta, and remove-after-a-later-upsert across two -- and assert the positive case as well, so the change cannot pass by never evicting anything: a peer removed while still owning its entries must leave the indexes empty. See PORTING.md section B, 'Rows'.

beads.title: Flag expired peers and re-evaluate expiry on a timer instead of only on netmap arrival
beads.description: Upstream's expiryManager (ipn/ipnlocal/expiry.go at commit a8b023c063b608fcead5446f3d885c4fc847c944) does three things this repository does none of. (1) flagExpiredPeers walks the netmap and, for every peer whose KeyExpiry has passed, sets Expired, clears Endpoints and HomeDERP, and breaks the node key with key.NodePublicWithBadOldPrefix -- defence in depth against control handing us an expired node that still looks live. Downstream, LocalBackend refuses a peerAPI dial to such a peer with "peer's node key has expired" and ipnstate.PeerStatus.Expired reports it to watchers. (2) nextPeerExpiry finds the soonest future expiry across the peers and the self node, and setControlClientStatusLocked arms a timer for it, so expiry is re-evaluated when it happens rather than whenever the next netmap arrives; commit 0640312e5 at this pin refreshes that timer's captured netmap from live peer state before reinstalling it, so a delta that arrived meanwhile is not rolled back. (3) onControlTime stores the delta between local time and MapResponse.ControlTime whenever it exceeds a minute, every expiry comparison is made against the adjusted time, and a delta-adjusted 'now' before a hardcoded epoch is ignored outright -- so a control server sending a wildly past ControlTime cannot expire the whole tailnet. Here, peer expiry is modelled and never enforced. ts_control::Node::key_expired and key_expired_at_unix exist and are correct (ts_control/src/node.rs), but their only callers are the SELF-node paths: the reauth decision in ts_runtime/src/control_runner.rs and Device::self_key_expired. No peer is ever flagged; ts_runtime::status::StatusNode (ts_runtime/src/status.rs) has no expired field for a watcher to read; nothing re-examines expiry between netmaps; and ts_control_serde::MapResponse::control_time (ts_control_serde/src/netmap.rs) is parsed off the wire and has no consumer at all, so there is no clock-skew correction either. The consequences are ordinary: this node keeps a fully configured WireGuard peer for a node whose key control has expired, keeps its endpoints and DERP home, keeps dialling it, and keeps accepting its peerAPI connections where a Go node refuses. Closing this bead means the flagging and the timer: a peer-side equivalent of flagExpiredPeers applied wherever the peer tracker installs peers, an expired field on StatusNode so the state is observable, the peerAPI refusal that reads it, and a nextPeerExpiry-shaped timer so a peer that expires between netmaps is caught. The ControlTime clock-delta correction is the part that makes it exact rather than approximate and may reasonably be split out, but it must then be filed before this bead is closed, because without it every comparison silently trusts the local clock. Note the two traps. First, the fail-closed direction here is to flag, not to drop: Go deliberately keeps expired peers in the netmap so callers can give a clear error, and removing them instead would lose that. Second, an already-expired peer must be skipped rather than re-flagged, or the log and the invalidation it triggers repeat on every netmap. Test with a peer whose expiry passes with no netmap in between -- that is the case the timer exists for -- and assert the negative case, that a peer with no expiry at all (a tagged node, KeyExpiry zero) is never flagged. See PORTING.md section B, 'Rows'.

beads.title: Treat REFUSED and SERVFAIL as soft errors when forwarding DNS to several upstreams
beads.description: At commit a8b023c063b608fcead5446f3d885c4fc847c944 upstream's DNS forwarder (net/dns/resolver/forwarder.go) treats both REFUSED (rcode 5) and SERVFAIL (rcode 2) as soft errors while a query is outstanding against more than one upstream resolver. SERVFAIL always was; REFUSED was added because a broken or misconfigured resolver answering REFUSED quickly could win the race and be handed to the client while a healthy resolver was still working, causing complete DNS failure. Only if every resolver refuses is the first REFUSED returned. The same commit also stopped replacing an upstream SERVFAIL with a locally synthesized packet and now returns the upstream's own bytes verbatim, because a synthesized answer throws away any RFC 8914 extended DNS error the upstream included. This repository has neither behaviour. ts_runtime::magic_dns::forward_query (ts_runtime/src/magic_dns.rs) walks its upstreams IN ORDER and returns cap_response(...) on the first datagram that came from the address it queried and whose header matches the query -- whatever RCODE it carries. So a first upstream that refuses ends the forward, the remaining upstreams are never tried, and the stub resolver is handed the refusal as though it were an answer. That bites exactly where a split-DNS route or a fallback list names more than one resolver, which is the common shape control pushes. The all-fail path is also weaker than upstream's: the caller's prebuilt SERVFAIL fallback is returned even when an upstream did answer SERVFAIL itself, so an extended error is lost. The change is contained in forward_query: keep going on REFUSED and SERVFAIL, remember the first such response, and return it only once the upstream list is exhausted, in preference to the synthesized fallback. The decision to make is whether to keep the sequential shape or move to Go's concurrent race. Sequential is the cheaper change and preserves this fork's one-overlay-socket-per-forward accounting (the MAX_INFLIGHT_FORWARDS semaphore assumes a bounded number of sockets per query); racing would match Go's latency behaviour but multiplies sockets per query and needs that bound revisited. Either is defensible -- say which was chosen and why. Test that a first upstream answering REFUSED does not stop the walk and the second upstream's answer is what reaches the client, and assert the two negative cases: every upstream refusing returns the first REFUSED verbatim rather than the synthesized SERVFAIL, and the existing anti-poisoning check still discards a datagram from the wrong source or with the wrong transaction id before any of this applies. Host-facing, not wire-facing. See PORTING.md section B, 'Rows'.

beads.title: Carry UserProfile.Groups off the wire so an embedder can authorise on group membership
beads.description: tailcfg.UserProfile at commit a8b023c063b608fcead5446f3d885c4fc847c944 carries a Groups field: 'a subset of SCIM groups (e.g. engineering@example.com) or group names in the tailnet policy document (e.g. group:eng) that contain this user and that the coordination server was configured to report to this node', always sorted when loaded from storage, and compared by UserProfile.Equal. It arrives in MapResponse.UserProfiles alongside ID, LoginName, DisplayName and ProfilePicURL, and Go surfaces the whole profile through WhoIs. ts_control_serde::UserProfile (ts_control_serde/src/user.rs) models the other four fields and stops there, so Groups is discarded at the wire boundary; ts_control::UserProfile (ts_control/src/node.rs) has nothing to carry it into, and ts_runtime::status::WhoIs flattens an owning user to a single display label resolved out of the peer tracker's accumulated profile table. This costs an embedded node more than it costs the daemon. The whole point of Runtime::whois is that an application can authorise an inbound tailnet connection by who opened it; group membership is the one attribute control offers for that which cannot be re-derived from anything else the node holds, so an embedder that wants it has to fetch it out of band. The wire half is mechanical -- a Vec<Cow<'a, str>> with serde default, since the field is omitempty and an older control server simply will not send it. The decision to make is how far up to carry it, because WhoIs currently reduces a profile to one String: either widen WhoIs to expose the profile (closer to Go's apitype.WhoIsResponse, and the shape that will keep absorbing future UserProfile fields), or add a narrow groups accessor and leave the flattening alone. Prefer the first unless there is a reason not to, and say why. Test that a profile with groups round-trips from a real MapResponse body through to what whois returns, and assert the absent case as well: a control server that omits the field must produce an empty group list, never a missing profile. See PORTING.md section B, 'Rows'.
